title: Bills to ban 287(g) agreements in Maryland could be on governor’s desk next week
summary: Maryland legislation to ban agreements between local law enforcement agencies and federal immigration authorities, specifically Immigration and Customs Enforcement, could be on Gov. Wes Moore’s desk by next week.
content:
by William J. Ford, Maryland Matters February 6, 2026

by William J. Ford, Maryland Matters February 6, 2026

Maryland legislation to ban agreements between local law enforcement agencies and federal immigration authorities, specifically Immigration and Customs Enforcement, could be on Gov. Wes Moore’s desk by next week.

The House Judiciary Committee voted 11-5 Friday to advance Senate Bill 245, sponsored by Sen. William C. Smith Jr. (D-Montgomery), just three days after it sailed through the Senate on a 32-12 vote.

The Senate Judicial Proceedings Committee voted 6-2 on Thursday to move the identical House Bill 444, sponsored by Del. Nicole Williams (D-Prince George’s). That bill had passed the full House just two days earlier, on a 99-40 vote.

Because each bill is an emergency measure, they need a three-fifths majority for passagre. Both exceeded that figure in their floor votes Tuesday.

“I’m super excited because … they’re both moving,” Del. J. Sandy Bartlett (D-Anne Arundel), chair of the Judiciary Committee, said Friday about the bills. “I hope the governor will sign [them] immediately.”

It appears he will.

Chorus of voices grows against possible ICE detention centers in Maryland

“I’m excited to have a bill that will come to my desk that will ensure that public safety is still going to be the number one priority for me and the number one priority for this administration,” Moore said to reporters Friday during an unrelated event in Howard County.

“We are going to do everything in our power to keep people safe, but that does not mean deputizing the people who are keeping people safe to go perform functions by a rogue ICE agency,” Moore said. “I’m looking forward to signing the bill that makes it to my desk.”

If signed next week, the emergency legislation would take effect immediately, giving legislative leaders one of their priority initiatives less than a month into the legislative session.

The 287(g) bills come amid a national debate over the aggressive immigration enforcement tactics adopted by the Trump administration, which led to the fatal shootings last month of two U.S. citizens in Minneapolis — Renee Good and Alex Pretti — by federal immigration officers.

Prior to those fatal shootings, a U.S. Border Patrol agent shot a Chicago woman five times in October. A month later, the federal government dropped its case against Marimar Martinez, and a federal judge on Friday granted permission for Martinez to share certain evidence from her case with the public.

Back in Maryland, nine counties have 287(g) agreements with ICE for detainers – allowing local officials to detain someone in their jails for an additional 48 hours for ICE to pick them up, if it is determined the person is in the country illegally.

Supporters of the agreements say the work is processed inside a local jail, which ensures there’s no danger to the community.

“This is not Minnesota. This is Maryland. We have programs in the state that are working,” said Sen. Jason Gallion (R-Harford and Cecil), who voted against the bill Tuesday. “I don’t understand why we would want to kind of kowtow to the national furor over what’s going on in another state by creating bad policy and removing a good program from this state.”

If the governor signs the legislation, the program would end in Allegany, Carroll, Cecil, Frederick, Harford, Garrett, St. Mary’s, Washington and Wicomico counties.

After the House approved the 287(g) bill Tuesday, Williams had a message for her constituents.

“This legislation helps to keep them safe,” she said. “So, while it’s not going to cure our broken immigration policy, it’s a step in the right direction for what we can do on the state level.”
